questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ at the point where $(\frac{\pi }{8},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot (2) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is $\sqrt{2}.$

The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by ${f}^{′}(0).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u={x}^{2}+2x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (2x+2) \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+2x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}+2\cdot 0-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $2\operatorname{cos}⁡1.$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2\pi -3x)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=2\pi -3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(-{csc}^{2}⁡u)\cdot (-3) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =3(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =3x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{8},1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot (2) \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$, we find 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-2\cdot {(\sqrt{2})}^{2} \\  & =-4\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is $-4.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function

$$
f = 2\sin u, \qquad u=3x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = 2\cos u, \qquad\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ if $y = 4\csc (5x + 3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = 4 \csc u, \qquad u = 5x+3.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = -4\csc u\cot u, \qquad\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-4\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot 5 \\  & =-20\operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u \\  & =-20\operatorname{csc}⁡(5x+3)\operatorname{cot}⁡(5x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we write

$$
f(x) = (\sin{x})^3.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f = u^3, \qquad u=\sin x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = 3u^2, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \cos{x}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3{u}^{2}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =3(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = \tan u, \qquad u = \sin x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \sec^2 u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The chain rule can be used to differentiate trigonometric functions like 

$$
y = \sin (2x).
$$

First, notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = \sin u, \qquad u = 2x.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot 2 \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=2x,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule can be used to differentiate trigonometric functions like

y = \sin (2x).
